item.title: Cyberattack on Austrian Foreign Ministry Exposes Diplomatic Staff Data
item.description:
Austrian Foreign Ministry Hacked, Staff Contact Details Accessed

Hackers accessed Austrian Foreign Ministry records containing staff contact details, including employees at diplomatic missions abroad.

Austrian Foreign Ministry confirmed a cyberattack against its website that exposed staff contact information, including details of employees working at diplomatic missions abroad. The security breach occurred between November 12 and 13, during a global Microsoft outage, and raises questions about the security of government websites and the risks associated with services managed by external providers.

According to the ministry, attackers gained unauthorized access to a website operated by an external service provider. The intrusion was detected on November 13, and authorities said they stopped it immediately.

“”Between November 12 and 13, the foreign ministry’s website, which is operated by an external service provider, was accessed in an unauthorized ​manner,” the ministry said in a statement, adding that it happened ​during a global Microsoft outage.” Reuters reports.

The ministry confirmed that the hack was detected on November 13 ⁠and government staff stopped it immediately.

An investigation by a team of cybersecurity experts found that the intruders had viewed records containing the names and professional contact details of ministry employees. The information covered both staff at the ministry’s headquarters in Vienna and personnel working at Austrian diplomatic missions abroad.

“An investigation by a team of experts ​found that during the unauthorized access, data records were viewed that listed ​the names and work contact details of employees at ministry headquarters as well as at diplomatic missions abroad,” the ministry added.

The Austrian authorities have not disclosed how many records were accessed, whether the attackers copied the information, or how they managed to enter the website. They have also not identified the vulnerability or attack technique used.

The ministry stressed that the incident did not affect citizens’ personal information. According to Austrian public broadcaster ORF, the authorities reported the incident to the Federal Office for Cyber Security and the Data Protection Authority, while also launching additional technical security checks.

“The Foreign Ministry emphasized that it was taking the incident “very seriously.” The integrity of the infrastructure was of the highest priority. The systems were subject to strict security regulations and continuous monitoring, it stated. The incident had also prompted additional technical security checks.” states ORF. “The Foreign Ministry has been repeatedly targeted by cyberattacks. At the beginning of 2020, there was a serious cyberattack that lasted until February. In April 2022, there were cyberattacks involving phishing emails.”

The timing of the incident is also noteworthy. The ministry said the intrusion coincided with a global Microsoft service outage, but it hasn’t established any connection between the two events. A major service disruption can complicate incident response and monitoring, but the available information doesn’t show that attackers exploited the outage to gain access.

Attribution remains another unanswered question. The ministry hasn’t named any suspected country or threat group, and there’s no evidence linking this particular intrusion to a state-sponsored operation.

However, the incident comes against a difficult diplomatic background. Austria has maintained military neutrality but has politically supported Ukraine since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. In July 2026, Vienna publicly accused Moscow of being responsible for a cyberattack against the Foreign Ministry in late 2019 and early 2020, joining eight other EU member states in condemning Russian cyber operations.

“The ministry did not suggest who might be responsible.” states Reuters.

Russia has repeatedly rejected Western accusations of hacking. Diplomatic tensions have also increased following Vienna’s decision to expel four Russian diplomats in October, bringing the total number of Russian diplomats declared persona non grata by Austria since 2020 to 18. Moscow promised an appropriate response and subsequently expelled an Austrian trade delegate working at the country’s embassy in Russia.

“Russia has repeatedly denied Western hacking allegations.” Reuters concludes.

Beyond the political context, this incident offers an important security lesson. Government websites may not host classified information or directly manage critical services, but they can still expose information that attackers can use to target employees, build convincing phishing campaigns, identify diplomatic personnel or gather intelligence about government operations.

The involvement of an external service provider also deserves attention. Outsourcing website management doesn’t outsource security responsibility. Public institutions need visibility into their suppliers’ security controls, access privileges, logging and incident response procedures, and must ensure that these arrangements receive regular independent checks.

Names and professional email addresses might appear to be low-value information, but they can help attackers prepare highly targeted operations. In diplomatic environments, even basic contact details can provide useful intelligence for social engineering and further intrusions.

Protecting government infrastructure also means protecting the people whose information and professional relationships can become the starting point for the next cyberattack.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Austrian Foreign Ministry)

Artificial intelligence is rapidly changing cybersecurity, reshaping both the techniques used by attackers and the tools available to defenders. item.title: Signal Is Blocking AI Agents From Reading Your Screen
item.description:
Signal is blocking OS-level AI agents from reading its app on iOS 27 and Android, warning that Gemini and Siri AI threaten its privacy guarantees.

Signal is restricting new AI agents built into iOS 27 and Android from capturing its data, president Meredith Whittaker announced. The company already did something similar on Windows last year, blocking screenshots to stop Microsoft’s Recall from capturing Signal messages by default. Now it’s doing the same wherever it can detect an AI assistant trying to read the Signal screen.

The process is simple, but it raises serious privacy concerns. Operating system-level AI agents, such as Google’s Gemini Intelligence and Apple’s Onscreen Awareness with Siri AI, scan the content displayed on your screen so they can answer questions and perform tasks for you.

This means these AI agents can capture your Signal data and use it to answer your questions and carry out your requests.

“In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents “scan” the information that’s on your screen. In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding.” reads the announcement. “The net result is that these AI capabilities in the operating system are undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy.”

Signal’s security model is based on open-source code and encryption that has been formally checked and reviewed by independent researchers for more than a decade. However, this protection can’t help if an AI agent reads your messages directly from the screen before encryption becomes relevant. Once captured, the data may be stored in a local database or sent to a remote server used by the AI agent, completely outside Signal’s control.

Google, Apple, and Microsoft aren’t just three companies among many here.

“these three operating systems are the oceans in which Signal, and other applications, must swim; they dictate the conditions of life for the application ecosystem.” continues the report. “Right now, these agentic AI integrations are changing this environment in a way that’s making it increasingly hostile to privacy.”

When the ocean starts working against the fish swimming in it, the fish can’t simply find a different ocean.

Signal’s fix is narrow: block screenshots on iOS 27, and block AI assistant screen capture attempts on Android. Users can turn the protection off in settings if they want to take screenshots, but doing so exposes their messages, and their contacts’ messages, to the same agents Signal is trying to keep out. The company is upfront that this doesn’t close every door, since an agent could still reach app data through the filesystem rather than the screen.

MacOS gets no protection at all right now, because Apple and Microsoft don’t give developers a clean way to block AI access without wrecking the normal user experience. Signal says it spent real engineering time just doing forensic work across Android and iOS to figure out what these AI systems actually do with app data, because the documentation isn’t there. That’s a strange place for a company Signal’s size to be: reverse-engineering the privacy behavior of the platforms it depends on.

Signal is asking Apple, Google, and Microsoft to take two specific steps. First, they should give app developers a clear way to prevent AI agents from accessing their data, including information on the screen, files, notifications, and APIs. Second, they should explain exactly how these AI agents access, collect, and process user data.

Signal also raises concerns about third-party AI agents such as Meta’s Muse, which can use accessibility permissions that users originally granted for other purposes. The company adds that confidential computing doesn’t solve the problem because the platform still controls the privacy decision, not the app developer or the user.

Signal says it’s already talking with Google and Apple about better support for apps that handle sensitive information. The company is cautiously optimistic, but whether these discussions lead to real changes will depend on what the two companies actually do over the coming year.

Signal frames the stakes plainly for anyone tempted to see this as one company’s problem.

“We all need to recognize that the current integration of AI agents into the operating system, without these common-sense remedies, represents an existential threat to privacy at the application layer, and the ability of independent developers like Signal to protect your sensitive data.” the report cocludes. “Signal is the canary in the coal mine, but this affects the entire ecosystem and should galvanize anyone who cares about these fundamental rights.”

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Signal)

item.title: Spain Stops NoName057(16) From Getting a Physical Foothold
item.description:
Spanish police arrested the alleged leader of NoName057(16) ‘s first physical cell in Spain, seizing weapons, ammunition and crypto wallets.

Spain’s National Police arrested a man in Burgos last Tuesday, calling him the main instigator behind what would have been NoName057(16)’s first physical cell in the country.

“The arrested man carried out propaganda, glorification and recruitment activities in favor of NoName057(16), and disseminated calls on social networks to cyberattack state institutions and confront the police.” reads the announcement published by the Spanish Police.

“This group claimed that the propaganda campaign it carried out in eight locations in Castile and León, Aragon, La Rioja and Madrid was the work of “its volunteers”.”

Until now, the pro-Russian group’s operations had been limited to cyberattacks. Spanish police say the arrest stopped plans to start violent activities. The suspect is being held on charges of belonging to a cyberterrorist organization and promoting terrorism.

“His arrest has thus far thwarted the start of violent attacks. This organization is believed to be responsible for at least 447 cyberattacks in Spain since 2014 against institutions, banks, and transport companies.” continues the announcement. “The arrested individual carried out propaganda, glorification, and recruitment activities on behalf of NoName057(16), and disseminated calls on social media to cyberattack state institutions or confront the police. He also acted as an intermediary for recruiting new supporters and referred interested parties to a recruitment system linked to NoName057(16). “

A search of his home uncovered much more than computer equipment. Police seized a semi-automatic rifle with a folding stock, several carbines and shotguns, high-capacity magazines, and more than 5,000 rounds of ammunition, including military-grade ammunition. Officers also found homemade clubs fitted with screws, double-edged detachable spears, brass knuckles, illegal pepper spray, chemical containers, and ten canisters of butanol. The discovery suggests that the suspect may have been preparing for activities beyond cyberattacks.

“The arrested man progressed from participating in online conspiracy groups to actively engaging in a channel where he promoted and glorified the group’s actions.” continues the report. “Last year, he distributed stickers bearing the organization’s emblem and QR codes that linked to its official channels in Burgos, Palencia, Lerma, Valladolid, Zaragoza, Logroño, Aranda de Duero, and Madrid.”

NoName057(16) isn’t a new name to Spanish authorities. The group has claimed at least 447 cyberattacks in the country since 2024, hitting institutions, banks, and transport companies. It formed in March 2022, shortly after Russia invaded Ukraine, with NATO members, the EU, and other Western allies as its stated targets.

The arrested man wasn’t directly involved in carrying out cyberattacks. Instead, he used social media to encourage attacks against government institutions and calls for confrontations with police. He also helped recruit new members by directing interested people to the group’s official recruitment system. In addition, he spread the group’s propaganda in eight locations across Castile and León, Aragon, La Rioja, and Madrid, handing out stickers with its logo and QR codes linking to its online channels.

Investigators say he gradually moved from following online conspiracy groups to running his own channel, where he praised the group’s activities. A court released him under certain conditions while the investigation continues. Police also found three physical cryptocurrency wallets containing bitcoin and are still investigating the origin of the funds.

The timing isn’t a coincidence on the political side either. On 16 November, the Council of the European Union sanctioned NoName057(16) under its cyberattack sanctions regime, freezing its funds and banning anyone from making resources available to it. A government can freeze an accounts and still not stop someone from stockpiling ammunition in Burgos, which is exactly the gap this arrest closes.

The case also lands days after Spanish courts ordered a full shutdown of the neo-Nazi group National Nucleus, sealing its headquarters in Burgos, Valladolid, and Madrid. Two unrelated extremist networks, one city, two closures in the same week. For a hacktivist group whose previous reach never left a browser tab, this represents the organization’s “first consolidated physical presence” in Spain.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, newsletter)

item.title: BADBOX 3.0 Exposed: Massive Botnet Hides Ad Fraud Inside Android TV Boxes
item.description:
BADBOX 3.0 returns with 40 billion daily ad requests, turning infected TV boxes into fraud machines

The BADBOX botnet is back, and its latest version has reached a scale that makes previous ad fraud operations look relatively small. Researchers from HUMAN’s Satori Threat Intelligence and Research team have uncovered BADBOX 3.0, a large-scale operation that uses infected Android-based TV boxes and other low-cost consumer devices to generate billions of fraudulent advertising requests every day.

“At its height, BADBOX 3.0 accounted for roughly 40 billion bid requests a day and more than 4% of all CTV traffic observed by the Human Defense Platform. BADBOX 3.0’s volume was more than three times the volume of the previous record holder, VASTFLUX, and represents a larger peak than the last five years’ worth of published Satori investigations combined.” reads the report published by Human.

“BADBOX 3.0 runs primarily on low-cost consumer devices infected with new backdoors that deliver fraud modules, including some that HUMAN researchers recognized from BADBOX and BADBOX 2.0.”

According to the investigation, the operation peaked at around 40 billion bid requests per day, accounting for more than 4% of all connected TV (CTV) traffic observed by HUMAN’s Defense Platform. That’s more than three times the volume attributed to VASTFLUX, the previous record holder.

The latest findings show that the operators haven’t simply rebuilt the previous botnet. They’ve expanded its capabilities by combining advertising fraud with the abuse of residential proxy networks, using the same compromised devices for both activities.

“The investigation began with a backdoor packaged as a system application with two hardcoded endpoints.” continues the report. “One endpoint retrieves the list of modules to load in the background, and the second handles logging.”

BADBOX 3.0 primarily targets inexpensive, off-brand Android devices, including TV boxes, smartphones and tablets running the Android Open Source Project (AOSP). Some of these devices reportedly arrive with backdoors already installed, allowing attackers to gain privileged access and install additional malicious components.

The advertising fraud works by running video ads in hidden windows. The infected device plays the ads in the background, while the malware generates advertising requests that impersonate legitimate connected TV applications. Advertisers and advertising platforms therefore receive what appears to be genuine traffic from popular streaming services, even though the applications being impersonated aren’t actually running on the infected devices.

“Modules delivered through BADBOX 3.0 mimic video ad software development kits (SDKs) and render the ads in a hidden window, so the ad plays on the device while the screen shows nothing unusual.” HUMAN researchers report. “The resulting bid requests present themselves as coming from well-known, legitimate CTV apps that the threat actors impersonated to route their traffic. “

The investigation also uncovered another revenue stream. The malware silently enrolls infected devices in residential proxy networks, turning their owners’ internet connections into infrastructure that third parties can rent and use.

Researchers identified 11 such networks, including ten commercially available services and PXYEDGE, a network allegedly operated by the same threat actors behind the BADBOX campaigns.

“One of those networks is PXYEDGE, the rebranded successor to the IpMoYu network exposed in BADBOX 2.0.” the report states. “Not all of the operation’s ad fraud requires an infected device: HUMAN also observed spoofed server-side ad insertion (SSAI) traffic monetized through many of the same supply paths.”

The device owner unknowingly provides the bandwidth and residential IP address, while someone else monetizes that access.

This creates a problem that extends beyond advertising fraud. Residential proxies can help criminals conceal the origin of their activities, making it harder to identify attacks involving account takeovers, fake account creation, payment card fraud and other forms of abuse.

The report also establishes a connection between PXYEDGE and IpMoYu, the residential proxy network previously exposed during the BADBOX 2.0 investigation. Researchers found overlapping infrastructure, proxy modules and task servers, concluding that PXYEDGE is likely IpMoYu operating under a different name. They also observed approximately 340,000 unique connections across monitored services, while the network advertised around 200,000 available nodes.

“The eleventh network is PXYEDGE, operated by the threat actors themselves and described below.” Human states. “Enrolling a device in these networks turns the owner’s home internet connection into a commodity without their knowledge or consent. The device owner pays for the bandwidth, and someone else sells access to the address. “

Another important finding concerns the infrastructure behind the operation. Satori researchers linked the BADBOX 3.0 malware catalog to TXCZ, a Chinese electronics manufacturer, through several independent technical connections.

These include command-and-control infrastructure, manufacturer-owned domains, preinstalled software, device-specific checks embedded in the malware and public code repositories used to distribute malicious modules. Researchers also identified a repository account incorporating TXCZ’s name and linked its maintainer to the threat activity.

These findings establish several connections between the malware infrastructure and the manufacturer. They don’t, by themselves, establish the extent of the company’s knowledge or involvement in the criminal operation.

The operators have also taken steps to make the botnet harder to disrupt. Instead of relying on a single download location, they distribute malicious modules through public code repositories and multiple backup hosting services. Some payloads are mirrored through an open-source content delivery network, while a self-hosted GitHub proxy helps devices retrieve files even when access to the original repositories is blocked.

This approach also gives researchers visibility into the malware’s development. By examining repository histories, Satori identified an actively maintained catalog containing hundreds of module versions, including components associated with earlier BADBOX campaigns and the vo1d malware family.

BADBOX has survived previous disruption efforts. Researchers first discovered the malware in 2023, when they found low-cost Android devices with a backdoor already installed in their firmware. In 2025, they uncovered BADBOX 2.0, a much larger operation that had infected more than 10 million devices across 222 countries and territories. Google, HUMAN, Trend Micro, Shadowserver and other partners then worked together to disrupt it. However, as BleepingComputer reports, the operators have returned with a new version.

HUMAN also joined a separate operation led by Google to disrupt XCPE, a related but different malware campaign. Researchers found more than one million infected devices in over 200 countries and territories. The operation also helped identify and take down several command-and-control domains used by BADBOX 3.0.

The researchers stress that disrupting the infrastructure doesn’t necessarily eliminate the threat. Previous investigations showed that the operators could rebuild their capabilities by moving to new servers, changing distribution methods and adapting their malware.

For consumers, the advice remains straightforward: buy devices from reputable manufacturers, check that Android devices are Play Protect certified, and install applications only through official marketplaces. Cheap, uncertified Android TV boxes deserve particular scrutiny, especially when their software and manufacturer cannot be independently verified.

The most important lesson from BADBOX 3.0 is that a consumer device can become part of a criminal operation without its owner noticing anything unusual. It can generate fraudulent advertising revenue, provide access to a residential internet connection and help conceal other malicious activities. The problem isn’t limited to the money lost by advertisers. It’s also about consumers unknowingly providing the infrastructure criminals need to operate.

“Each chapter of this research has ended with a version of the same observation: disrupting an operation and dismantling the conditions that produced it are different achievements.” the report concludes. “BADBOX 3.0 shows what that intact supply chain produces. The capability now lives in public code repositories, mirrored across hosting platforms, a mainstream CDN, and a proxy built to slip past network blocks, with fallback locations written into every module record. Its proxy network survived exposure by changing its name. Its ad fraud, hidden on the devices and passed off under the names of legitimate apps, reached a daily volume larger than any ad fraud operation disclosed before it.”

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, newsletter)

item.title: Bulgaria Discovers Massive Government Breach After Five Years of Undetected Spying
item.description:
Bulgaria uncovered a five-year cyberespionage campaign that stole 130GB of government files. The attacker and full impact remain unknown.

Bulgaria ‘s ministry for innovation and digital transformation announced it had uncovered a hacking operation running since 2021. Reuters reports that more than 130 GB of documents, about 62 million pages, were downloaded from government databases over those five years. Minister Ivan Vassilev said there’s no evidence so far that Bulgarian citizens’ personal data was compromised.

“The minister, Ivan Vassilev, said that since 2021 more than 130 GB, ​or 62 million pages, of documents had ​been downloaded, but that there was no evidence ⁠so far that Bulgarians’ personal data had been compromised, ​Nova TV reported on its website.” Reuters reports.

The breach came to light only after Bulgaria introduced a new national cybersecurity monitoring system, which spotted suspicious activity in August. Until then, the country apparently had no system in place capable of detecting an intrusion that had been going on since 2021. This raises questions not only about the attackers’ capabilities but also about the lack of security monitoring inside government networks.

Several international hacking groups may be behind the attack, but investigators haven’t linked it to any specific country or nation-state actor. The stolen files reportedly include cabinet documents, reports and communications between ministries and government agencies.

“We discovered that several international hacker groups had accessed Bulgarian systems starting in 2021,” Vassilev said. “The information they stole included sensitive details of how Bulgarian state institutions operate”

“At this stage, there is no evidence that the personal data of Bulgarian citizens has been affected,” the minister added.

After the attack was discovered, several agencies joined the response, including intelligence services, the defense ministry, police, cybersecurity experts and international partners such as the EU’s cybersecurity agency. Authorities have isolated the affected systems, blocked the attackers’ access and removed the malware. Prosecutors have also been informed. Vassilev wants them to investigate not only the hackers but also whether government agencies failed to detect the intrusion earlier.

The government also has questions to answer. Bulgaria went through several unstable governments and repeated elections during the five years the attackers remained inside its systems. This political instability may have affected long-term investment in cybersecurity. An attack that went unnoticed from 2021 to 2026 doesn’t only raise questions about the attackers’ skills. It also highlights how weak security monitoring allowed them to stay hidden for so long.

This isn’t first time Bulgaria faced a major breach, and the contrast is worth noting. In 2019, hackers stole roughly 11 GB of data from the National Revenue Agency, exposing personal details on nearly five million citizens, about 71% of the population at the time, and a Russian link was floated before a 20-year-old local suspect was arrested. This time the target was institutional correspondence rather than citizen records, and the scale of documents taken, 130 GB against 11 GB, dwarfs that earlier case.

What’s missing from Wednesday’s announcement is almost everything that would let the public judge the real damage: who did this, what specific documents went out the door, and whether any of it has already been used. Bulgaria’s own cybersecurity agency, BTA, described the find as “Government Uncovers Apparent Years-Long Breach of Administrative Networks”, language that tells you an investigation is still very much open, not closed.

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, Bulgaria)

item.title: Microsoft Entra Connect Health Breach Exposes Tenant Metadata and Admin Details
item.description:
Microsoft Entra Connect Health breach exposed tenant metadata and admin details, potentially enabling targeted phishing and social-engineering attacks.

Microsoft has disclosed a data breach involving its Entra Connect Health service, which exposed tenant metadata and administrator contact details.

“On 9 November 2026, we detected a vulnerability in the Microsoft Entra Connect Health API that was introduced on 23 July 2026. The vulnerability could allow an unauthorized party to access tenant and service-monitoring metadata and potentially make changes to Connect Health monitoring configuration.” the company wrote on Reddit.

Microsoft Entra Connect Health is a cloud service that helps administrators monitor the health, performance and alerts of their on-premises identity systems. The IT giant says no passwords, authentication tokens or valid cryptographic keys were compromised, but the exposed information could still help attackers craft convincing phishing and social-engineering attacks.

The issue came from a vulnerability in the Entra Connect Health API, introduced on July 23, 2026. Microsoft identified the flaw on November 9 and deployed a server-side fix on November 19.

“We deployed and fixed the vulnerability on 19 November 2026. On 20 November 2026, we concluded our investigation and determined that unauthorized read-only access to tenant-level metadata associated with your organization had occurred. We did not identify any unauthorized configuration changes.” the IT giant added.

Customers do not need to install a software update because Microsoft addressed the problem on its side.

The attackers could only view the data, but the exposure still created risks. They gained access to administrator email addresses, tenant IDs, domain names and synchronisation status. Attackers could use this information to plan targeted attacks and impersonate Microsoft support staff, service providers or internal IT administrators.

Microsoft has not disclosed how many tenants were affected. However, several administrators and managed service providers have reported receiving notifications from the company, suggesting that the breach may have affected many customers.

Microsoft says no software update or customer remediation is needed because the Entra Connect Health API vulnerability has been fixed. However, it recommends several precautionary steps. Organisations should alert security and IT teams to possible targeted phishing and social-engineering attempts, ensure administrator accounts use phishing-resistant MFA, and apply Privileged Identity Management for just-in-time access.

They should also run Microsoft’s read-only PowerShell script to review potentially exposed metadata, check Connect Health settings, and examine Entra audit logs, sign-in logs and Azure Activity Logs for suspicious activity. Microsoft advises verifying the security notice directly through Azure Service Health rather than clicking email links.

item.content:encoded:
Microsoft Entra Connect Health breach exposed tenant metadata and admin details, potentially enabling targeted phishing and social-engineering attacks.

Microsoft has disclosed a data breach involving its Entra Connect Health service, which exposed tenant metadata and administrator contact details.

“On 9 November 2026, we detected a vulnerability in the Microsoft Entra Connect Health API that was introduced on 23 July 2026. The vulnerability could allow an unauthorized party to access tenant and service-monitoring metadata and potentially make changes to Connect Health monitoring configuration.” the company wrote on Reddit.

Microsoft Entra Connect Health is a cloud service that helps administrators monitor the health, performance and alerts of their on-premises identity systems. The IT giant says no passwords, authentication tokens or valid cryptographic keys were compromised, but the exposed information could still help attackers craft convincing phishing and social-engineering attacks.

The issue came from a vulnerability in the Entra Connect Health API, introduced on July 23, 2026. Microsoft identified the flaw on November 9 and deployed a server-side fix on November 19.

“We deployed and fixed the vulnerability on 19 November 2026. On 20 November 2026, we concluded our investigation and determined that unauthorized read-only access to tenant-level metadata associated with your organization had occurred. We did not identify any unauthorized configuration changes.” the IT giant added.

Customers do not need to install a software update because Microsoft addressed the problem on its side.

The attackers could only view the data, but the exposure still created risks. They gained access to administrator email addresses, tenant IDs, domain names and synchronisation status. Attackers could use this information to plan targeted attacks and impersonate Microsoft support staff, service providers or internal IT administrators.

Microsoft has not disclosed how many tenants were affected. However, several administrators and managed service providers have reported receiving notifications from the company, suggesting that the breach may have affected many customers.

Microsoft says no software update or customer remediation is needed because the Entra Connect Health API vulnerability has been fixed. However, it recommends several precautionary steps. Organisations should alert security and IT teams to possible targeted phishing and social-engineering attempts, ensure administrator accounts use phishing-resistant MFA, and apply Privileged Identity Management for just-in-time access.

They should also run Microsoft’s read-only PowerShell script to review potentially exposed metadata, check Connect Health settings, and examine Entra audit logs, sign-in logs and Azure Activity Logs for suspicious activity. Microsoft advises verifying the security notice directly through Azure Service Health rather than clicking email links.

item.title: Cleverbridge Confirms Attackers Copied Payment Card Data From Its Platform
item.description:
Cleverbridge confirms attackers stole payment card numbers, expiry dates and CVV codes, warning customers to watch for fraudulent transactions.

Cleverbridge, which runs checkouts, payments and subscriptions for other companies, has confirmed that attackers copied payment card data from its platform. The company says it found the problem on 4 November and started notifying affected people on 20 November. That’s a gap of 16 days.

“On 4 November 2026, Cleverbridge detected unauthorised activity in our platform and took immediate steps to contain the incident.” reads the incident update published by the company. “Whilst our investigation remains ongoing, regretfully, we have been able to determine that a third party copied payment card data stored on our platform.”

Affected systems went offline for a short time and were back online the same day. Only later did the investigation show that a third party had copied payment card data stored on the platform, and the company says that the investigation is still running.

The company’s website lists customers such as SUSE, Red Hat and Parallels, but the company has not said which businesses were affected.

If you bought a product or service from a company that uses Cleverbridge, it may have handled your payment and stored your card details. Cleverbridge provides payment and subscription services to software and SaaS companies.

Cleverbridge has not clearly explained what information was stolen on its public incident page. It says the exposed data may include payment card details and directs affected customers to check their individual notifications. However, a notification reviewed by BleepingComputer provides more details: the stolen information may include card numbers, expiration dates and CVV or CVC security codes.

That last item is the one that matters. The card industry’s own rules generally bar companies from keeping the security code once a payment is authorised, so BleepingComputer asked Cleverbridge why the codes were accessible at all.

The company did not disclose technical details about the attack, however, its answer excluded a ransomware attack.

“None of our systems were encrypted.” continues the update.

Cleverbridge says it hired TransUnion/Cyberscout, a third-party vendor, to support the notifications, and that a notice sent on its behalf is legitimate. It has offered credit or identity monitoring where available, with sign-up details in the notice. Asked why people weren’t told sooner, it says it moved fast and notified them without undue delay.

Cleverbridge advises users to watch for phishing attempts and warns that it will never request card details, passwords or security codes by email, phone or text.

“As always, we recommend that our users follow general best online security practices, remain vigilant, and be aware of phishing attempts.” the company states. “Out of an abundance of caution, please be cautious of unexpected emails, calls, or messages about this incident. Cleverbridge will never ask you for your card details, passwords, or security codes by email, phone, or text message. ”

Call your card issuer sooner rather than later. Cleverbridge says the issuer may decide to replace your card after you report the incident.

We recommend that you check your card statements carefully and tell your card issuer right away about any transaction that you do not recognise.” concludes the report. “You may also wish to contact your card issuer to tell them about this incident and follow any advice they give, as they may decide to replace your card. ”

Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon

Pierluigi Paganini

(SecurityAffairs – hacking, payment card data)
